depth: Across the five frames, the monocular depth map depicts a cluttered garage or utility area as the camera wearer turns and proceeds toward a side doorway. In Frame 1, the brightest feature is a dark hanging coat or draped fabric on the left, positioned within arm's reach at about 0.3–0.6 m and partly blocking a sink counter with potted plants roughly 2.5–3 m back. That counter is around 1–1.5 m left of a closed door and a refrigerator approximately 2–2.5 m away on the right, while a scooter handle and table edge appear lower in the view at about 1 m. From Frames 2 through 4, the wearer turns left and moves down the corridor toward the rear garage door, which is about 5–7 m ahead. The wall, doorway frame, and shelving on the right come within reach at roughly 0.5–1.2 m, as a person wearing dark clothing walks ahead about 2.5–3.5 m away and around 1–1.5 m to the right of the central clutter. The person faces away and right toward the doorway and never looks back at the wearer. By Frame 5, the open white interior door and the right doorframe dominate the foreground at an arm's-reach distance of about 0.4–0.8 m, blocking the room beyond apart from a dark gap approximately 2–3 m away. Relative to the motion-blurred RGB images, the depth output distinguishes the foreground wall surface, recessed doorway, central clutter heaps, and deep background corridor more clearly. Still, it becomes unreliable in Frame 2, where intense motion blur reduces the walking person and floor to an unclear mid-grey wash, and in Frame 4, where the person entering the recessed doorway merges almost completely with the depth of the surrounding doorframe.
segmentation: Only a limited selection of objects is identified by the instance segmentation map throughout the garage sequence, and Frames 2 and 4 contain no detections at all. In Frame 1, the map incorrectly marks the dark hanging garment at the extreme left as a "person." It is approximately 0.3–0.6 m away, within the camera wearer's reach, and clipped by both the left and bottom borders. The map also identifies two "potted plant" instances on the counter about 2.5–3 m ahead, positioned slightly above waist height and roughly 1.5 m left of the fridge, plus the "refrigerator" on the right around 2–2.5 m away, whose lower-right portion is obscured by a foreground table. In Frame 3, the true "person" is segmented about 3 m ahead and just right of center, oriented away and toward the right, with their right arm within reach of the doorway approximately 0.4 m in front of them. Every nearby shelf, plant, and item of floor clutter is missed. In Frame 5, when the wearer reaches within 0.4–0.8 m of the doorway, the open white paneled door on the left is wrongly classified as a "refrigerator." The dark figure in the doorway opening on the right, about 1.5–2 m away and roughly 0.5 m right of the door panel, is facing away into the connected room and is divided into two incomplete "person" masks cut off by the right doorframe. Segmentation makes the moving person's outline against the cluttered shelving in Frame 3 clearer and reveals the small potted plants in Frame 1 that visually merge with the RGB background. Nevertheless, it is very unreliable because of false-positive categories—the coat is called a person and the door a refrigerator—and total detection loss under motion blur in Frames 2 and 4.
pose: Frames 1, 2, 4, and 5 contain entirely empty pose maps; only Frame 3 displays a single yellow upper-body skeleton, and no frame contains any magenta hand skeletons. In Frame 3, the detected skeleton places the walking person at middle range, about 3 m ahead of the camera wearer and slightly to the right of the central aisle. They stand immediately left of the side doorway and roughly 1–1.5 m to the right of the cluttered table. The head, shoulder, torso, and right-arm keypoints indicate that the person is turned away from the wearer and angled toward the doorway on the right. They are looking forward into that doorway rather than turning back toward the camera, and their lifted right forearm reaches to within about 0.3–0.5 m—arm's reach—of the door-handle area. Their lower body is not mapped and is partly blocked by clutter in the foreground. Compared with the motion-blurred dark clothing visible in the RGB frame, the skeletal overlay makes the person's forward torso lean, head direction, and raised-right-arm pose in Frame 3 substantially easier to interpret. Even so, the pose result is mostly unreliable over the full sequence: motion blur, low lighting, and heavy obstruction from clutter and doorframes cause the system to miss the person entirely in Frames 2, 4, and 5, while also failing to capture the person's legs and hands in Frame 3.
